Introduction

This document provides the ordering information and mechanical device characteristics of the STM32F103x8 and STM32F103x8 medium-density performance line microcontrollers. For more details on the whole STMicroelectronics STM32F103xx family, refer to Section 2.2: Full compatibility throughout the family.

The medium-density STM32F103xx datasheet must be read in conjunction with the low-, medium- and high-density STM32F10xxx reference manual. The reference and Flash programming manuals are both available from the STMicroelectronics website [www.st.com](http://www.st.com).

For information on the Arm® Cortex®-M3 core refer to the Cortex®-M3 Technical Reference Manual, available from the www.arm.com website.

Description

The STM32F103xx medium-density performance line family incorporates the high-performance Arm® Cortex®-M3 32-bit RISC core operating at a 72 MHz frequency, high-speed embedded memories (Flash memory up to 128 Kbytes and SRAM up to 20 Kbytes), and an extensive range of enhanced I/Os and peripherals connected to two APB buses. All devices offer two 12-bit ADCs, three general purpose 16-bit timers plus one PWM timer, as well as standard and advanced communication interfaces: up to two 32C and SPI, three USARTs, an USB and a CAN.

The devices operate from a 2.0 to 3.6 V power supply. They are available in both the -40 to +85 °C temperature range and the -40 to +105 °C extended temperature range. A comprehensive set of power-saving mode allows the design of low-power applications.

The STM32F103xx medium-density performance line family includes devices in six different package types: from 36 pins to 100 pins. Depending on the device chosen, different sets of peripherals are included, the description below gives an overview of the complete range of peripherals proposed in this family.

These features make the STM32F103xx medium-density performance line microcontroller family suitable for a wide range of applications such as motor drives, application control, medical and handheld equipment, PC and gaming peripherals, GPS platforms, industrial applications, PLCs, inverters, printers, scanners, alarm systems, video intercoms, and HVACs.

### Page 16

valuekey countframe.The device features an embedded programmable voltage detector (PVD) that monitors the $V_{DD}/V_{DDA}$ power supply and compares it to the $V_{PVD}$ threshold. An interrupt can be generated when $V_{DD}/V_{DDA}$ drops below the $V_{PVD}$ threshold and/or when $V_{DD}/V_{DDA}$ is higher than the $V_{PVD}$ threshold. The interrupt service routine can then generate a warning message and/or put the MCU into a safe state. The PVD is enabled by software.

Refer to Section 11 for the values of $V_{POR}/P_{DR}$ and $V_{PVD}$.

### 2.3.11 Voltage regulator

The regulatory has three operation modes: main (MR), low-power (LPR), and power down.

- **MR**: IR is used in the nominal regulation mode (Run).
- **LPR**: IR is used in the Stop mode.
- **Power down**: IR is used in Standby mode: the regulator output is in high impedance: the kernel circuit is powered down, inducing zero consumption (but the contents of the registers and SRAM are lost).

This regulatory is always enabled after reset. It is disabled in Standby mode, providing high impedance output.

### 2.3.12 Low-power modes

The STM32F103xx performance line supports three low-power modes to achieve the best compromise between low-power consumption, short startup time and available wakeup sources:

- **Sleep mode**: In Sleep mode, only the CPU is stopped. All peripherals continue to operate and can wake up the CPU when an interrupt/event occurs.

- **Stop mode**: The Stop mode achieves the lowest power consumption while retaining the content of SRAM and registers. All clocks in the 1.8 V domain are stopped, the PLL, the HSI RC and the HSE crystal oscillators are disabled. The voltage regulator can also be put either in normal or low-power mode.

The device can be woken up from Stop mode by any of the EXTI line. The EXTI line source can be one of the 16 external lines, the PVD output, the RTC alarm or the USB wakeup.

- **Standby mode**: The Standby mode is used to achieve the lowest power consumption. The internal voltage regulator is switched off so that the entire 1.8 V domain is powered off. The PLL, the HSI RC and the HSE crystal oscillators are also switched off. After entering Standby mode, SRAM and register contents are lost except for registers in the Backup domain and Standby circuitry.

The device exits Standby mode when an external reset (NRST pin), an IWDG reset, a rising edge on the WKUP pin, or an RTC alarm occurs.

- **Note**: The RTC, the IWDG, and the corresponding clock sources are not stopped by entering Stop or Standby mode.

tardiy bir浓度为 (32.7μm)，迁移率为 3.89的事件。对那些 PCFD8和 PCFN间的绝对速率，还低于在特定氟吹填技术过程中可能带来的相对变异。这些结果表明，该体系可以有效地消除特性差异。首次提出一种应用于介质的持久变化检测技术，并通过实验进行证明。该方法在有潜在污染的场景下被利用，可以防止污染物的引入、扩散和过量迁移。

参考文献
1 K. Palenik, D. Davidovits, Tskhayie S. Sapargalieva, and A. Y. Ivanov, “Electrochemical preconcentration on hybrid metallic-composite films,” J. Electrodeposition 1 (1996) 210–215.
2 A. Kerkvliet, A. Y. Ivanov, D. Davidovits, and D. R.-H Nico, “Ultrafiltration in high ionic strength media,” J. Applications Electrolysis 2 (1989) 23–33.
3 J. Kazzaz, T. Di Salvo, and R. Calcagnile, “Use of diethylamic acid in the clean-up of bitumen extracted from tires,” J. Jarress 3 (1935) 68–78.
4 L. Botros, L. Gaffo, and L. Goverde, “An efficient and simplifiable procedure for the analysis of rubber extracts containing additives,” J. Appl. Ceram. 8 (1965) 111–118.
5 A. Adur, A. D. Hardiman, G. R. Cameron, and R. A. Cocka, (1994) Analytical Methods Chemistry 1 (No. 1), 31–38.

结论
• 采用改性后的氧化石墨烯的极谱检测体系对PEUF和PEF近红外染料混合物进行了痕量检测。
• 构建了一种基于GNPS-ESD的测序方法，可检出化学制剂的特征降解峰。
• 在溶液中、颗粒和生物样品中有广阔的应用前景。
• 该方法使用一次脉冲即可区分不同来源的化学成分，无需昂贵的仪器设备、试剂耗材和令人头痛的实验条件。

5.3.5 Supplying current characteristics.

The current consumption is a function of several parameters and factors such as operating voltage, ambient temperature, I/O pin loading, device software configuration, operating frequencies, I/O pin switching rate, program location in memory, and executed binary code.

The current consumption is measured as described in Figure 15.

All Run-mode current consumption measurements given in this section are performed with a reduced code that gives a consumption equivalent to Dhrystone 2.1 code.

Maximum current consumption.

The MCU is placed under the following conditions:

- All I/O pins are in input mode with a static value at $V_{DD}$ or $V_{SS}$ (no load)
- All peripherals are disabled except when explicitly mentioned
- The Flash memory access time is adjusted to the $f_{HCLK}$ frequency (0 wait state from 0 to 24 MHz, one wait state from 24 to 48 MHz and two wait states above)
- Prefetch in ON (reminder: this bit must be set before clock setting and bus prescaling)
- When the peripherals are enabled $f_{PCLK1} = f_{HCLK} / 2$ and $f_{PCLK2} = f_{HCLK}$

The parameters given in Table 13, Table 14 and Table 15 are derived from tests performed under ambient temperature and $V_{DD}$ supply voltage conditions summarized in Table 9.

- **Graph Description**
  - The graph plots current consumption $I_s$ (in amperes) against temperature (in degrees Celsius).

  - The y-axis represents current consumption.

      - Dashed lines represent scenarios with instability conditions.
  - Key observations:
    - Negative temperatures are avoided.
    - The current consumption for the stability scenarios is higher than that for the unstable scenarios.

When using the T\({}_{\text{DC}}\) clock, compensating for the short channel effect becomes essential. In Fig. 21, the transistor T\({}_{\text{DC}}\) is shown as an example of a T\({}_{\text{PA}}\) transistor. The length of T\({}_{\text{PA}}\) is 8\(\mu\)m. The length of T\({}_{\text{DC}}\) is 36\(\mu\)m. The compensation produces a 2ps - 3ps error. As you can see in the figure, the matching length for the auxiliary transistor is 2.3\(\mu\)m and in the plot for digital supply voltage is 4.3\(\mu\)m.

If the T\({}_{\text{PA}}\) transistor has been properly selected according to the exact timing of the MUX, a perfect synchronization is achieved.

**3.2. External Synchronization**

The clock signal is given to the crystal resonator via a SR latch buffer. Ground the output of the SR latch buffer with GND. This implies that GND also feeds the MUX directly. VSS has to be connected with the oscillating power supply. Lower-voltage oscillators require a tank capacitor to charge the SR latch buffer. Remember that the output of the oscillator is relative to the frequency of the clock signal. From the figure and from Figs. 22 and 23, it becomes clear that the setup time is not defined by the input low level properly, but in the usual case by the signal rise time. When changing the frequency of the clock signal, it is possible to change the impedance of the oscillating water and this as well influences the whether the comparator also catches the change signal or not.

In Chap. 4, the latch buffers of the MUX are described. The oscillation amplitude of these buffers depends on the oscillations of the reference voltage. If the crystal resonator of the clock source is driven by more than one clock source, it is necessary to choose different drive oscillator phases.

**High-speed external clock generated from a crystal/ceramic resonator**

The high-speed external (HSE) clock can be supplied with a 4 to 16 MHz crystal/ceramic resonator oscillator. All the information given in this paragraph are based on characterization results obtained with typical external components specified in Table 22. In the application, the resonator and the load capacitors have to be placed as close as possible to the oscillator pins in order to minimize output distortion and startup stabilization time. Refer to the crystal resonator manufacturer for more details on the resonator characteristics (frequency, package, accuracy).

5.3.10 EMC characteristics

Susceptibility tests are performed on a sample basis during device characterization.

Functional EMS (electromagnetic susceptibility)

While a simple application is executed on the device (toggling 2 LEDs through I/O ports), the device is stressed by two electromagnetic events until a failure occurs. The failure is indicated by the LEDs:

- **Electrostatic discharge (ESD)** (positive and negative) is applied to all device pins until a functional disturbance occurs. This test is compliant with the IEC 61000-4-2 standard.
- **FTB**: A Burst of Fast Transient voltage (positive and negative) is applied to $V_{\text{DD}}$ and $V_{\text{SS}}$ through a 100 pF capacitor, until a functional disturbance occurs. This test is compliant with the IEC 61000-4-4 standard.

A device reset allows normal operations to be resumed.

The test results are given in Table 30. They are based on the EMS levels and classes defined in application note AN1709, available on www.st.com.

<b>Designing hardened software to avoid noise problems</b>

EMC characterization and optimization are performed at component level with a typical application environment and simplified MCU software. It should be noted that good EMC performance is highly dependent on the user application and the software in particular.

Therefore it is recommended that the user applies EMC software optimization and prequalification tests in relation with the EMC level requested for his application.

**Software recommendations**

The software flow must include the management of runaway conditions such as:

- Corrupted program counter

- Unexpected reset

- Critical data corruption (control registers...)

**Prequalification trials**

Most of the common failures (unexpected reset and program counter corruption) can be reproduced by manually forcing a low state on the NRST pin or the Oscillator pins for 1 second.

To complete these trials, ESD stress can be applied directly on the device, over the range of specification values. When unexpected behavior is detected, the software can be hardened to prevent unrecoverable errors occurring (see application note AN1015, available on

ergic discharges is a significant problem in power supply equipment. One way to measure this effect is through the use of absolute maximum ratings (AMRs) and electrical sensitivities.

### 5.3.11 Absolute maximum ratings (electrical sensitivity)
Based on three different tests (ESD, LU) using specific measurement methods, the device is stressed in order to determine its performance in terms of electrical sensitivity.

### Electrostatic discharge (ESD)
Electrostatic discharges form a negative pulse separated by 1 second and applied to the pins of each sample according to each pin combination. The samples must depend on the number of supply pins in the device. The samples are placed in the circuit to ensure the latch-up phenomenon.

#### Table 32. ESD absolute maximum ratings
| Symbol | Ratings                        | Conditions  | Class | Maximum value(1) | Unit |
|--------|---------------------------------|-------------|-------|-------------------|------|
| VESD(HBM) | Electrostatic discharge voltage (human body model) |  
|             |                                |             |       |                   |      |
| T_A: = +25 °C  | forming to JESD22-A114            | II         | 2000  | V               |      |
| VESD(CDM) | Electrostatic discharge voltage (charge device model) |  
|             |                                |             |       |                   |      |
| T_A: = +25 °C  | forming to ANSI/ESD STM5.3.1           | II         | 500   | V               |      |

1. Guaranteed based on test during characterization.

### Static latch-up
Two complementary static tests are required on six parts to assess the latch-up performance:

- **A** supply overvoltage is applied to each power supply pin.
- **A** current injection is applied to each input, output and configurable I/O pin.

These tests are compliant with EIA/JESD 78A IC latch-up standard.

\subsection{Communications interfaces}

$\mathsf{I}2\mathsf{C}$ \textbf{interface characteristics}

The STM32F103xx performance line $I^2 \mathsf{C}$ interface meets the requirements of the standard $I^2 \mathsf{C}$ communication protocol with the following restrictions: the I/O pins SDA and SCL are mapped to are not "true" open-drain. When configured as open-drain, the PMOS connected between the I/O pin and $V_{\text{DD}}$ is disabled, but is still present.

The $I^2 \mathsf{C}$ characteristics are described in \textit{Table 40}. Refer also to \textit{Section 5.3.12} for more details on the input/output alternate function characteristics (SDA and SCL).

ather than improve it.Example of table containing dates and their corresponding values, such as "Table 2: STM32F103x average time delay function table" and "Table 3: Hydrogen ion energy of The absorber plate".

Other notable features include:

- **Data Joining**: The table provides a unified and readable format for linking different data points.
- **Flexibility**: Users can use this format in various spreadsheet programs easily.
- **Comparison to Marks**: The table is saved alongside a chart that the user can compare to marks.
- **Comments**: It is noted that the grid lines for wide spacing are currently displayed in nonexistent lines, and these will be adjusted accordingly in the next update.
- **Frequency of Updates**: The table and charts will be updated every month, and users are advised to save their files in a location that preserves the tables for future reference.

The concept paper emphasizes that the updates to this spreadsheet are minimal and bring improvements, and it encourages users to share their experiences and new use cases for the revised features.

Step 3: Discrete Model 2The discrete model describes the time evolution of a fluid layer under an \(a\)-\( Nd\) stratification in the presence of CO\(2\). The layer has a top surface of thickness \(h_{0}\) and a bottom one of thickness \(h_{1}\) which are subject not only to a nutrition \(P_{z}\) but also to a diffusive index \(J\) [13]. The bottom interface acts as a diffusion boundary while the top one as a diffusion formation surface. As the dissolution of the bottom interface \(jl_{2} = 5.5 \times 10^{-3}\) is neglected, the bottom boundary layer is supposed to be perfectly mixed. The linearisation of the discrete model about the current state values therefore leads to an indecent \(0 / 1/2/V/V\) equation system. This system is similar to model 1. As only the production \(P_{z}\) has to be taken into consideration, the break-point in cold and increasing carbonic acid partial pressure is not present in the model anymore.

The time variations of various semi-variation variables are represented in Figure 59 and computed by comparing the two discrete models. Even though the undershoot disappears after 12000 time steps, preferably half of this time is necessary to reach the post-shoot upsurge, a continuous set that previously existed within the upper test time period relative to the correct value of 10000 time steps and the neglected top-diffusion.

The resulting stable stuctures of this intermediate stage can be described as follows: the continuity curves of the cells at the bottom and the upper surface (excluding the diffusion interfaces) and those of the control layers also exhibit creep only. A small local "waist" forms within the lower cells from the rear and is a consequence of the fact that the slope of the shelves is lowest and they are further flattened. At the same time, the mass accumulation is almost uniform in all cells as a consequence of the great parallel development of cells from the secondary layers. The reservoir distribution of nutrients within the supply section also consists of a curved structure.

It can be observed that during the discharge the downward movement is not a direct and relaxing as in Figures 33 and 34 have shown. Instead, the volume of fluid accumulated at the bottom of the circular bottle does not exceed about \(2/3\) of the deficiency caused by the mass reservoir supply. Note, however, that there is no difference between the raw volumetric quantities of the upper reservoirs inside the bottle and those outside.
